Puzzle 12 · 13 of 17

Where images live on disk

Puzzles 9 to 11 followed layers from a tar archive to an overlay mount. Here's where Docker keeps them in between, why an image takes more disk than its download, and how to tell which of Docker's two ways of storing images your machine uses.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 8: Who builds the container?

    The docker command only sends a request to dockerd. dockerd hands the container to containerd, which starts a shim; the shim runs runc with config.json, the OCI runtime spec's description of the container. runc asks the kernel for the namespaces and the cgroup, starts the program and exits, leaving the shim as its parent. After that, the container is the process the kernel runs, and nothing else.

    Review puzzle 8

  • Puzzle 10: Stacking layers into one tree

    The overlay filesystem shows read-only lower directories (the image's unpacked layers) and one writable upper directory as one merged tree. New files land in upper; the first write to a file from a lower layer copies the whole file up first; a deletion becomes a whiteout in upper. The lower layers never change, which is why one image can serve many containers.

    Review puzzle 10

The problem

Puzzle 9's alpine:3.20 downloaded 3.6 MB, and its layer unpacks to 8.1 MB of files. On the run behind this page, docker image ls said it takes 12.2 MB. That's neither number: more than both. And puzzle 10's mount line listed directories with long containerd names, while older guides point to a different folder altogether. Which is right, and where do your images really live?

See it

The building block

Docker has two ways to keep images, and a machine uses one of them.

The containerd image store is the default for Docker Engine 29 and later on new installations. It hands image storage to containerd (the program from puzzle 8), which keeps each layer twice:

  1. Compressed, exactly as it was downloaded, in its content store: on the test machine, Alpine's layer is the file …/io.containerd.content.v1.content/blobs/sha256/25f1d6b1951a…, 3,630,321 bytes.
  2. Unpacked, as a directory of plain files, prepared by a snapshotter: the containerd component that turns layers into directories (snapshots) and stacks them for a container. The default snapshotter is overlayfs; Alpine's layer became …/snapshots/1/fs, 8.1 MB, the directory you saw as a lowerdir in puzzle 10.

That's why docker image ls shows two sizes:

$ docker image ls alpine:3.20
IMAGE         ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
alpine:3.20   d9e853e87e55       12.2MB         3.71MB

Content size is what was downloaded (the compressed layer plus a few small JSON files); disk usage counts the compressed copy and the unpacked one. Docker's documentation says it plainly: the containerd image store uses more disk space because it stores images in both compressed and uncompressed formats. In return, it can keep images for several kinds of processor and the extra files some images carry (puzzle 16), and save or upload an image without packing its layers again. The two copies have different jobs: containers mount the unpacked snapshot, while docker save and uploading the image (puzzle 14) need the compressed blob; Docker's documentation warns that with content missing, save can produce an incomplete archive and uploads can't send the missing layers.

The older way is a storage driver. Installations upgraded from before Docker 29 keep using one until someone switches, and on Linux it is almost always overlay2. It stores only the unpacked layers, under /var/lib/docker/overlay2, and builds the same kind of overlay mount for each container. The mechanism of puzzles 10 and 11 is the same with either: read-only lower directories, one writable upper directory per container.

Which one does your machine use? docker info says:

$ docker info --format '{{.Driver}} {{.DriverStatus}}'
overlayfs [[driver-type io.containerd.snapshotter.v1]]

"overlayfs" with driver-type io.containerd.snapshotter.v1 is the containerd image store with its overlayfs snapshotter. "overlay2" would be the storage driver. On the test machine dockerd started its own containerd, so the store sits under /var/lib/docker/containerd/daemon/; where it sits on yours depends on how containerd runs there, which is one more reason to trust docker image ls and docker system df rather than walking the folders. Docker's documentation also warns against changing anything under /var/lib/docker by hand.

Two edges. The containerd image store doesn't work with puzzle 5's userns-remap setting, so a daemon using that keeps the storage driver. And switching between the two doesn't move images: Docker's documentation says the other backend's images and containers stay on disk but become hidden until you switch back.

The analogy

The building keeps two copies of every delivery: the sealed box exactly as the courier brought it, on a shelf in the post room, and the unpacked furniture laid out in a storeroom, ready to show through any flat's floor. The old building kept only the unpacked furniture: less room, but nothing to hand straight back to a courier.

Run it yourself

On a Linux machine with Docker. Predict, before running, whether your disk usage is bigger than your content size, and which storage your daemon reports.

docker info --format '{{.Driver}} {{.DriverStatus}}'
docker pull alpine:3.20
docker image ls alpine:3.20
docker system df

With the containerd image store, expect disk usage well above content size, as above. With overlay2, docker info prints overlay2 and its own details instead.

Check yourself

A machine with the containerd image store pulls an image whose layers are 200 MB compressed and 600 MB unpacked. Roughly how much disk does it take?

Right. Both copies stay.

Not quite. The snapshotter unpacks them when the image is pulled.

Not quite. That's the older storage driver; the containerd store keeps both.

A teammate's docker info shows Storage Driver: overlay2; yours shows overlayfs with driver-type io.containerd.snapshotter.v1. What differs?

Right. Same overlay mounts, different storage of layers.

Not quite. Each layer is still its own directory, stacked for each container.

Not quite. Both build the same overlay mount: lower directories and one upper.

On the containerd image store, the compressed blob of an image's layer goes missing from the content store, but its snapshot is still there. Can a container from that image still read its files?

Not quite. A compressed tar can't be mounted; containers use the snapshotter's directory.

Right. Containers use snapshots; save and push use blobs.

Not quite. Running needs only the snapshot; saving and pushing are what need the blob. Re-read that part ↑

What you now know

Docker 29 keeps images in the containerd image store by default on new installations: each layer is kept compressed, as downloaded, in containerd's content store, and a snapshotter (overlayfs) unpacks it into a directory that becomes a lower directory. So an image takes its download size plus its unpacked size. Installations upgraded from older Docker keep the overlay2 storage driver, which stores only the unpacked layers; docker info tells you which one you have.
